summary: Introduces the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol, which gives routers a two-way, event-driven channel to their radio modems. Through it, the router learns changing link characteristics such as speed and state so it can make better routing decisions.

eli5.summary: A walkie-talkie tells the driver how good the signal is right now, so the driver can choose the best road.

questions: how routers learn radio link quality
how do routers learn radio link quality
subtitle: How a router and its radio or satellite modem keep each other posted on changing link speed, delay and reachability.

tldr.problem: Routers that rely on modems for wireless links need timely knowledge of link speed, state and reachable neighbors, but manual configuration or inference through routing and transport protocols cannot keep up with mobile conditions.
tldr.mechanism: DLEP opens a session between a router and its modem: UDP multicast discovery, then a TCP connection that carries messages in which the modem reports destinations and metrics such as data rate and latency as they change.
tldr.outcome: The router learns about neighbors arriving or leaving and about link quality as events happen, so it can route better. Extensions are negotiated per session.

today: RFC 8175 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Variable Links
sections.content:
Modems for line-of-sight radios, satellite terminals and broadband links can change speed and quality from moment to moment, because of multipath interference, obstructions, rain fade and similar effects. Speed can also differ per destination and per traffic type. The RFC's example is an 802.11 access point serving two laptops: one may have 54 Mbps for unicast while the other has only 32 Mbps, and multicast goes at the base rate, usually 24 Mbps or less.

Link connectivity may also come and go without changing the router's interface state, and IP routing protocols tend to depend on interface state and timers such as HELLO messages. With a modem attached over Ethernet, the router cannot see events on the radio link or the real capacity. The Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) runs between a router and its attached modem to report link characteristics and convergence events, meaning the acquisition and loss of potential routing next hops. It is event driven, and it runs over a local one-hop TCP session, which guarantees delivery of the event messages.
sections.eli5: A car's dashboard does not know that the road ahead is flooded. DLEP is like a friend on the radio who tells the driver as soon as the road changes, instead of waiting until the car gets stuck.

sections.title: Routers, Modems and Destinations
sections.content:
DLEP runs only on the local link between a router and a modem. How modems signal to each other over the air is not specified and is a matter for the modem implementer. If a router has several modems, or a modem has several connections, there is a separate session for each.

The session carries information about destinations, which are addressable places reachable over the link. A destination can be physical, such as a far-end router, where the MAC address is that of the far-end router and not of the modem. It can also be logical, such as multicast, where the Layer 2 address derived from the Layer 3 address is treated like any other destination.

The requirements are strict about scope. DLEP MUST be implemented on a single Layer 2 domain, MAC addresses MUST be unique within a session, and implementations MUST support the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (RFC 5082). Discovery uses UDP multicast and messages use TCP. Using IPv6 link-local addresses is RECOMMENDED. The RFC describes dedicated deployments (direct cables or a dedicated switch) and networked deployments, where Layer 2 tunneling must enforce the single-hop requirement.
sections.eli5: Each router has a private line to its own modem. Over that line the modem tells the router who it can reach, like a list of friends within shouting distance.

sections.title: The Session Life Cycle
sections.content:
A DLEP participant goes through five states: Peer Discovery, Session Initialization, In-Session, Session Termination and Session Reset. Modems MUST support Peer Discovery. Routers MAY support discovery or rely on preconfigured TCP address and port information, in which case they start in Session Initialization.

In discovery, a router sends Peer Discovery Signals repeatedly, with 60 seconds RECOMMENDED as the interval and 1 second as the minimum. A modem listens on the DLEP well-known multicast address and port and MUST reply with a Peer Offer Signal, which can carry connection points. The router then opens a TCP connection, preferring IPv6 connection points and preferring connection points that use TLS. TLS SHOULD be used, and for networked deployments it is STRONGLY RECOMMENDED.

In initialization the router sends a Session Initialization Message and the modem answers. A Success status moves both sides to In-Session. In-Session, messages flow both ways until one side sends a Session Termination Message. Termination waits for a Session Termination Response (a sender SHOULD allow 4 heartbeat intervals), then Session Reset releases resources, drops the destinations without sending Destination Down Messages, and closes TCP. If the TCP connection ends unexpectedly, the implementation goes straight to Session Reset.
sections.eli5: It is like a phone call: you look for each other, you say hello, you talk, you say goodbye, and then you hang up and tidy up before the next call.

sections.title: Destinations, Metrics and Heartbeats
sections.content:
After initialization the modem tells the router about destinations. A modem MAY send a Destination Up message for a new reachable destination, and the router replies with a status: 0 Success to receive more information or 1 Not Interested. A router can instead send a Destination Announce for a destination it cares about, typically multicast, but modems SHOULD use Destination Up where they can. Destination Down reports that a destination is no longer reachable. A modem SHOULD send Destination Update when something changes, and that message has no response.

Metrics describe the link: maximum and current data rate in each direction (64-bit values in bits per second), latency in microseconds, Resources (0 to 100, such as battery), Relative Link Quality in each direction (0 to 100) and MTU. The modem declares all metrics it will use, with default values, in the Session Initialization Response, and using a metric it did not declare is an error. Metrics can be session-wide (Session Update) or per destination (Destination Update), and the most recently received value wins. A router can also send a Link Characteristics Request to ask for a different data rate or latency, and the modem answers with the resulting values or with 2 Request Denied.

Heartbeat Messages keep the session alive and check two-way connectivity. 60 seconds is RECOMMENDED and 1 second is the minimum. Any valid message resets the timer, and a peer MUST allow at least 2 intervals of silence before ending the session with status 132 Timed Out. Only one request per destination may be outstanding at a time, and transactions do not time out.
sections.eli5: The modem keeps shouting 'friend A just came into range, and the signal is this strong!' and 'friend B left!'. If neither side says anything for a while, they check the other is still there, and hang up if not.

sections.title: Signals, Messages and Data Items
sections.content:
DLEP has two kinds of protocol units. Signals are used only in discovery and ride in UDP datagrams. Messages go both ways over TCP. Both are a header followed by an unordered list of Data Items, and Data Items are TLV (Type-Length-Value) structures with a 16-bit type and a 16-bit length. All integers MUST be in network byte order.

A Signal header starts with the four characters DLEP, then a 16-bit Signal Type and a 16-bit Length that counts only the Data Items. A Message header has just the 16-bit Message Type and Length. There are two Signals (Peer Discovery is type 1 and Peer Offer is type 2) and 16 Messages. Data Item types run from 1 (Status) to 20 (MTU), with 65408 to 65534 reserved for private use.

Error handling is blunt. An unrecognized or unexpected Signal is ignored, as is a Signal whose TTL is not 255. An unrecognized Message gets a Session Termination with status 128 Unknown Message, an unexpected one gets 129, bad data items get 130 Invalid Data, and a Message about an unannounced destination gets 131 Invalid Destination. Status codes below 100 mean Continue, and all others mean Terminate.
sections.eli5: Every note starts with a label that says what kind it is and how long it is, then a list of small labeled facts. If a note makes no sense, the receiver says so and hangs up.

sections.title: Extensions and Experiments
sections.content:
No extension is required for an implementation to be DLEP compliant. Extensions add Messages, Data Items or status codes with their rules, and they are negotiated per session. Each side lists what it supports in the Extensions Supported Data Item during initialization, and after that it MUST NOT use anything that the peer did not list. Interoperable extensions need to be standardized as an update to this document or as a separate specification.

The Private Use ranges in the registries allow experiments, which MUST be announced as extensions using Private Use extension identifiers agreed in advance. Using several experiments in one session is discouraged because their definitions could clash. For scale, the protocol is intended to support thousands of destinations per modem and router pair, and implementations should consider dampening flapping devices and hysteresis for small quality changes, though the RFC leaves those algorithms out of scope.
sections.eli5: Both sides agree on which extra tricks they know before they start, and use only tricks both know. There is a play area for trying new tricks, as long as both agree first.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC lists three concerns: an attacker pretending to be a DLEP participant, altering Data Items so the receiver's view of the network is wrong, or joining an unsecured radio network and injecting signals that make a router forward traffic to the wrong place. The impact depends on how much DLEP data feeds the control plane. For example, bogus data could cause poor route selection or wrong policing decisions.

The RFC therefore wants security at the transport layer and at Layer 2. With TLS, each peer SHOULD check the credentials of the other, and the RFC points to RFC 5487 for pre-shared keys in dedicated deployments and RFC 7525 for networked ones. At Layer 2 it suggests IEEE 802.1AE and 802.1X. The Secured Medium flag in the Peer Type Data Item lets a router judge how far to trust a modem, and an untrusting router SHOULD consider limiting the size of attached subnets it uses for route selection. Against denial of service, it is RECOMMENDED to remember hosts that repeatedly fail Session Initialization and ignore their later Peer Discovery Signals.

IANA created the DLEP registries and assigned port 854 for TCP and UDP, the IPv4 multicast address 224.0.0.117 and the IPv6 multicast address FF02:0:0:0:0:0:1:7.
sections.eli5: If a stranger could pretend to be your radio friend, they could send you the wrong way. So both sides should check who they are talking to, and the line between them should be locked.
